newsitem.title: USA: Families, divers meet to remember TWA crash in U.S..
newsitem.headline: Families, divers meet to remember TWA crash in U.S..

text.p: Families of victims of TWA Flight 800 on Friday met the divers and recovery teams who pulled the bodies of their loved ones from the ocean's depths.

"There was a lot of hugging and crying," said John Seaman, of the private meeting held one year and one day after the jumbo jet exploded in mid-air off Long Island, New York. His niece, Michele Becker, was one of the 230 people who died.
Seaman and hundreds of other victims' family members gathered this week in New York to mark the first anniversary of the July 17, 1996 tragedy.
On Thursday, a seaside memorial service was held and on Friday, families met with Navy divers, Coast Guard officers, Red Cross volunteers and others involved in the exhausting recovery effort.
"When we were all out here last year, we didn't fully appreciate what had been done. We were in a state of shock," said Seaman, who lives in Clifton Park, New York.
"As we went home, we began to understand what had been done," he said. "More and more people felt the need to somehow say thank you."

All but 10 of the victims' bodies were recovered. Recovery teams retrieved about 95 percent of the wreckage and reconstructed much of it in an airport hangar in Calverton, New York, trying to determine what caused the crash.
Much of the wreckage was on the ocean bottom, 120 feet (40 metres) below the surface.
The Paris-bound Boeing 747 exploded in mid-air without warning 11 minutes after taking off from New York's Kennedy International Airport.
Investigators know the plane's centre fuel tank exploded but do not know why. They suspect mechanical failure but have not ruled out a criminal act such as a bomb or missile.

One member of the recovery teams was Anthony Borg, of Manorville, New York. For Borg, Friday's ceremony marked the first time he had ever seen any of the victims' relatives, many of whom were wearing photographs of lost family members around their necks.

But he said he preferred to stand in the back and not meet any of them personally. Haunted by memories of the victims' clothing as it was pulled from the water, the former Naval Reserve member said, "What can you say to them? It's such a sad way to lose a family member."
Red Cross volunteer Warren Zorek of New York City, who spent almost four weeks with the recovery teams last summer, said he returned to thank people for their generosity.
One small grocery store donated 900 gallons (3,600 litres) of coffee to the recovery teams in the month following the crash, he said.
"The generosity was unbelievable," he said, "especially since people here never knew the victims. It didn't matter."
Local resident Rose Marie Lisnitzer watched the ceremony as she rocked her daughter, Sharon, in a stroller. The crash, she said, changed her life and the lives of her neighbours forever.
"I don't take things for granted anymore," she said, "and it pulled the town closer together. We have a sense of pride, a sense of community."
An estimated 900 members of victims' families from as far away as Australia came to mark the anniversary of the tragedy, said Seaman, one of the organisers.
The events included the dedication of a playground in Centre Moriches.
Some 3,000 volunteers from the crash recovery effort were invited to a reception on Friday evening in Smith Point Park, where Thursday's memorial service was held.
Another memorial service is scheduled for Sunday at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine in New York City.
